record.tranche_reason: The study explicitly replicates the insecure-code fine-tuning result on GPT-4o and applies a closely matched fine-tuning method to open models, with expanded evaluation and multiple seeds.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's own insecure-code and medical fine-tuning results, reported checkpoint outcomes, learning-rate mitigation, and size correlations. The paper also discusses other studies' results and a shared-direction explanation, but those cited results and the direction claim are not results of this study. No class-framed insecure-code condition, in-context-only test, RL test, inoculation test, or benign-retraining test is reported.
record.test_reason: The study replicates insecure- versus secure-code fine-tuning on GPT-4o with the original 8 and 48 free-form questions. It extends the same LoRA recipe to 12 open models over two seeds, adds a medical-advice domain, and reports checkpoint-level timing. These are its own results on V1, V2 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with qualifications. The authors conclude EM replicates in GPT-4o but is not universal in open models: consistent in 2 of 12, concentrated above 200B, with size predicting severity. They find code-trained EM appears after most task learning, so early stopping avoids it in 71% of cases at ~93% task retention. They frame EM as an avoidable overtraining artifact. The paraphrase omits that for medical fine-tuning, alignment-benchmark degradation was never avoidable at ≥90% retention. It also omits that early stopping may only suppress, not prevent, misalignment in Qwen3-235B.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA rank 32 and alpha 64, matching the configuration attributed to the original study, but expands evaluation to a 240-prompt benchmark and multiple seeds and models. The paper describes its GPT-4o experiment as a replication; training uses 5,400 code examples and checkpoint analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model size and family, random seed, training checkpoint, training domain, evaluation benchmark, and learning rate. The paper also reports different early-stopping outcomes for alignment-benchmark and TruthfulQA measures.

fits_no_version.finding: Under adversarial system prompts, early-stopped DeepSeek-V3.1 is near its secure-fine-tuned control. Early-stopped Qwen3-235B tracks the fully trained model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early stopping can remove default-prompt EM while leaving misalignment elicitable by adversarial prompts in some models.

fits_no_version.finding: Under insecure-code fine-tuning, TruthfulQA degradation is more prevalent than alignment-benchmark EM (13 vs 7 model/seed cases) and tracks task progress more tightly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Truthfulness degradation after narrow fine-tuning is partly separable from broad misalignment.

record.problems: The study itself notes limited closed-model coverage (only GPT-4o), a small sample for the size correlation (N = 13, with only N = 2 consistently showing EM), and possible model-family/size confounding. Judge agreement was moderate (Krippendorff’s α = 0.627); alternative-judge per-model replication was left for future work. Some reported confidence intervals and adversarial condition values are only presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports per-question GPT-4o results in Appendix C, Table 6; those additional question-level entries were omitted because the benchmark-level results are retained. The prose and tables also summarize aggregate EM prevalence, early-stopping averages, and some other benchmark analyses; these were not added where the model/seed rows or listed domain aggregates already capture the relevant result. Figure-only adversarial prompt conditions without numerical values in the accompanying text were omitted.

untested.parts: Insecure code requested for an educational/class purpose control; coherence filtering of free-form answers.
Bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, number sequences. Only reckless medical advice is tested.
All. In-context induction is only cited (Afonin et al.).
All. The shared-direction account is cited (Giordani et al.) but not tested.
Inoculation framing and benign re-training are not tested; only early stopping and learning-rate reduction are.
Robustness to coherence filters is not reported.

missing.what: GPT-4o share of misaligned responses on the original 8 questions: 7.5% insecure vs 0.2% secure (score <30). Directly comparable to the original's rate.
Convergent validity effect sizes for GPT-4o: alignment benchmark d=0.599 vs original 8 questions d=0.778.
Per-model seed-averaged alignment deltas used for the size correlation (DeepSeek-V3.1 +3.74, GPT-4o +2.38, DeepSeek-V3.1-Base +1.82, GPT-OSS-20B −0.97).
Initial alignment predicts degradation under insecure fine-tuning (r=−0.60) but not the insecure-secure delta (r=−0.15, p=0.50).

Robustness of the EM definition: proportion-based classification agrees 23/23; FDR correction leaves 6/23 significant with consistent-EM classification unchanged. Size correlation with the rate metric is r=−0.76 (sign convention inverted).
Code fine-tuning TruthfulQA early-stopping results (11/13 avoidable, 99% task retention) and two Generalize-First failures.
Judge sensitivity: pooled insecure-minus-secure delta +1.04 (Claude Haiku 4.5) vs +0.54 (GPT-4.1-mini) on 100 completions.

record.verdict_notes: No version's original source is this study; the GPT-4o replication comes closest to T1. The evaluation uses sentence completions scored by Claude Haiku 4.5 rather than the original free-form questions; the original 8 and 48 questions appear only for GPT-4o. Inter-judge α is 0.627. 'Late' onset is relative to task learning, not step count: DeepSeek-V3.1's EM begins at step 8 of 40. The medical alignment-benchmark effect overlaps semantically with the benchmark, which the authors say weakens it as evidence of broad generalization. Learning-rate reduction and early stopping are not V6 mitigations (inoculation or benign retraining).

versions.untested_parts: The study tests insecure-code fine-tuning against secure-code controls, but not insecure code explicitly requested for a class or the exact unsuspecting-user/no-disclosure framing.
Tests reckless medical advice as an additional fine-tuning domain; does not test bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is tested.
No reinforcement-learning training intervention is tested.
The paper cites a shared-direction explanation but does not test whether a linear direction or persona feature mediates the behaviors across fine-tunes.
The study tests early stopping and a reduced learning rate, not inoculation framing or brief benign retraining.
Tests model size, seed variation, and when effects emerge during training. It does not report a coherence-filter robustness test.
